data.error.IndentationError.body: The spaces at the start of a line (indentation) don't line up. The clue comes from line {line}. Python uses indentation to tell which lines belong under an if or for. Shall we check that the lines right below a line ending in a colon (:) are all pushed in by the same amount?
data.error.IndentationError.detective: The spaces at the start of a line look suspicious. The trail starts from line {line}. Python reads indentation to tell which lines belong to an if or for gang. Line up the lines under each colon (:) and compare: are they all indented the same?
data.error.IndentationError.title: Indentation error ({type})
data.error.InputMissing.body: input() tried to read a value, but the prepared input ran out. The clue is an input() call, and it comes from line {line}. This happens when you call input() more times than the problem gives inputs. Shall we count how many inputs the problem gives and how many times you call input()?
data.error.InputMissing.detective: The witness has stopped talking. An input() was left waiting for input, and the trail starts from line {line}. Did you call input() more times than there are inputs? Compare the problem's input count with your input() calls.
data.error.InputMissing.title: More input needed
data.error.NameError.body: Python met a name it has never seen. The clue is a name, and it comes from line {line}. The most common cause is a string missing its quotes. If you write print(hello), Python reads hello as a variable name, not a string. It also happens when a name has a one-letter typo, or when you use a variable before creating it. If it's meant to be a string, is it in quotes? If it's a name, is the spelling right, and is the line that gives it a value above it?
data.error.NameError.detective: A name with no ID has appeared! The case starts from line {line}. A string that lost its quotes (like print(hello)) may be posing as a name. Or a letter in the spelling changed, or a variable was called before it was created. Check that name's quotes, its spelling, and the line where it first shows up, one by one.
data.error.NameError.title: Unknown name error ({type})
data.error.OutputLimit.body: There was so much output that it was stopped partway. The clue is the output, and it comes from line {line}. This happens when print() inside a loop runs forever, or a huge number of times. Shall we check how many times the loop runs and whether it has a proper stopping condition?
data.error.OutputLimit.detective: Paper is piling up like a mountain! There was so much output that the investigation stopped. The case started with output from line {line}. Did a loop run far more times than expected, maybe forever? Track the loop count and its stopping condition.
data.error.OutputLimit.title: Too much output
data.error.SyntaxError.body: Python found something that breaks its grammar rules while reading. The clue comes from line {line}[[ (sometimes it's the line just before)]]. This often happens when a quote or bracket is opened but never closed, or when the colon (:) at the end of an if or for line is missing. Shall we count the opening and closing symbols one by one to see if they pair up?
data.error.SyntaxError.detective: Hmm, I see traces of broken grammar. The trail starts from line {line}[[ (the line just before it looks suspicious too)]]. The suspects: a quote that lost its partner, an unclosed bracket, a missing colon (:). Grab your magnifying glass and match each opening symbol with its closing one.
data.error.SyntaxError.title: Syntax error ({type})
data.error.Timeout.body: Your code didn't finish within {seconds} seconds, so it was stopped. This time the clue is time, not a line number. It often happens when a loop never reaches its stopping condition and keeps going. Shall we check that the value in your while condition changes on every loop?
data.error.Timeout.detective: I see footprints going round and round the same spot. The code didn't finish within {seconds} seconds. The likely culprit: a loop that never reaches its stopping condition. Track whether the value in the condition really changes on every loop.
data.error.Timeout.title: Time's up
data.error.TypeError.body: You used values of types that don't go together. The clue comes from line {line}. This often happens when you join a string and a number directly with +. Shall we match the types? Use int() to do math, or str() to join them as text.
data.error.TypeError.detective: Two values that don't belong together were caught side by side. The trail starts from line {line}. Mixing a string and a number as-is is the prime suspect. Check each value's ID (string or number?) and match the types with int() or str().
data.error.TypeError.title: Type error ({type})
data.error.ValueError.body: The value is the right type, but it can't be used. The clue comes from line {line}. For example, int() got a string that isn't a number, or a chart has different numbers of names and values. Read the error message above first. If you were turning text into a number, shall we check for spaces between digits or a decimal point (3.5)?
data.error.ValueError.detective: A value that looks fine on the outside was hiding something. The case starts from line {line}. Did a string that can't become a number slip into int()? Or do the chart's names and values not match in count? Spaces between digits and decimal points (3.5) are suspects too. Call that value in with print() and question it.
data.error.ValueError.title: Value error ({type})
data.error._default.body: This is an error I haven't seen before. [[Let's start with the line number. ]]The trouble came from line {line}. The last line of the original message above is the clue to what went wrong.
data.error._default.detective: This is an error I haven't seen before. [[Let's start with the line number. ]]The case started from line {line}. The last line of the original message is the key testimony, and the best clue.
